title: Chalmers warns of Hanson, Coalition threats to super
full_text:
Treasurer Jim Chalmers has thrown down the gauntlet to the government's political opponents over compulsory superannuation, vowing to defend the scheme after One Nation leader Pauline Hanson said she wanted more Australians to be able to dip into their retirement savings early.
The $4.5 trillion sector, twice the size of the economy, is the largest source of private cash savings in Australia and is designed to alleviate pressure on the federal budget by enabling people to support themselves in retirement.
Liberal senator Andrew Bragg provoked the compulsory super stoush last week by declaring it "one of the biggest public policy failures since federation" and likening super for teens to super for cats and dogs. Senior Coalition MPs yesterday also backed people having more control over their retirement savings.
Chalmers sounded the alarm yesterday morning, framing the debate as existential to Australians' economic security and accusing his political opponents of seeking to destroy the system.
"The stakes are high at the next election for a whole range of reasons, and one of them now is the future of Australia's world-leading compulsory superannuation system," Chalmers said as he arrived at Parliament House.
"The Liberals, the Nationals, and One Nation would end compulsory superannuation as we know it. Their policy and their ideology on super would absolutely decimate the economic security and retirement incomes of millions of Australian workers.
"They share a dangerous and divisive anti-worker, anti-super ideology, and if this plays out after the next election, Australian workers will be much worse off."
Chalmers said the existing allowances for Australians to withdraw their super early were well considered and available for people in genuine hardship.
Labor pursued the fight in question time yesterday, asking consecutive Dorothy Dixer questions about super to launch attacks on the Coalition and One Nation.
"Not only do they want to drag Australians back to the past, they want to damage their future as well," Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said.
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said his party supported people "having flexibility to invest their superannuation as they see fit".
Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson, a long-time critic of union links to superannuation, said reducing the 12 per cent contribution rate in exchange for increased wages was "not [the Coalition's] focus" but that Australians should have greater control over investments.
"The Labor Party believes that superannuation money is their money," he told News24, formerly Sky News.
Hanson joined the fray on Sunday, saying super "should be lightened up a bit" so people can withdraw money in times of crisis.
"In some ways, I feel that you should give them their money now and ... help them with the cost of living. It is their money. They've sacrificed it in lieu of pay, so in a lot of cases people want it," Hanson told News24.
Compulsory superannuation contributions are paid as part of an employee's salary.
However, Hanson suggested that people spent their super and still ended up on the aged pension.
"I think the whole system is broken," she said.
Hanson was forced to clarify her position in a post on social media, saying she was not calling for an end to compulsory super but that Australians "should be able to access their money more easily if they need it for a house, medical needs or other costs".
Asked yesterday where the line would be drawn for what constituted a crisis, One Nation treasury spokesman Barnaby Joyce said the party was still developing its policy.
Association of Superannuation Funds of Australia chief executive Mary Delahunty said early access to super penalised people twice by taxing savings at a higher rate and leaving less at retirement.
She said using funds for house deposits was inflationary because it stimulated demand, and early access also increased reliance on the aged pension.
"Calling super a policy failure ignores the objective facts. From 2002 to 2022, poverty among over-65s fell from about 30 per cent to 11 per cent because of super."
The Super Members Council said in a statement a 30-year-old who withdrew $20,000 today would have about $93,000 less at retirement because of lost compound investment returns.
Nationals Senate leader Bridget McKenzie said about 60,000 people facing financial hardship had withdrawn from their super each year, but said it should not come to that. "You shouldn't be having to access your retirement savings to get through the normal financial issues of a week," she told News24.
